en: Taking much gold and many possessions,
They shared it out in celebration;
They took gold and ornaments by the pud,
And carried away great wealth.
“Kyyaz has taken Chürök,” they said;
The people clamored, and his prestige rose.
The Jediger, glutted with riches,
Could scarcely open their eyes.
Then warrior Kyyaz
Reached the broad expanse of Jeti-Özön,
At the wooded slope of Jerge-Talduu,
And pitched his royal camp.
At the spur where the mountain divides,
Where Toltoi kept watch,
Upon a rounded ridge,
Across the broken, rolling hills,
On the far-facing slope,
Beside the hillock
With forty birches and twin poplars,
He reached the place and pitched his royal camp.
Kyyaz, warrior of the Jediger,
Brought Aichürök’s white yurt,
Its crown-ring golden and its ropes of brass;
Thus it came into warrior Kyyaz’s hands.
He became a man of imposing rank;
Warrior Kyyaz struck fear into hearts
And became khan over all the people.
In warrior Kyyaz’s hands
Lay immeasurable wealth and myriad goods;
He became their boundless owner,
A giant who ruled the people,
A khan who maintained a royal court,
A man of exceptional power—
Such was warrior Kyyaz.
He became lord of the people he ruled;
Such was warrior Kyyaz’s station.
Dear hero Kyyaz—
Dust rose wherever he rode,
And souls fled before his might.
He became a renowned man;
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
Accomplished Kyyaz became khan.
“In Talas I, Kyyaz of the Argyn,
Utterly destroyed the people,” he said;
“I slaughtered them without leaving one.
Only Kanchoro, my sworn brother for the life to come,
Did I leave alive.
I stripped the country bare with plunder;
Not merely the bloodthirsty hero’s livestock—
I seized his wife as well.
In fertile Keng-Köl and broad Talas
I strangled every settled man.
I avenged the blood-price not of one brother but seven,
Pursuing their vengeance to the full;
Before Allah I have no regret.
I brought death upon his people;
Not merely his ordinary livestock—
I seized the bloodthirsty hero’s wife.”
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
“Let all my settled people come,” he said.
“Let them see my wedding feast,
And what I intend for my people;
Let all who wish behold it.
Let them call me a hero unequaled in the world;
Let my people witness my valor.”
In the lowlands of Jeti-Özön
Accomplished Kyyaz pitched his yurt.
“For the feast at which I take a wife,
Let all my people come without exception;
Let every soul witness
The bridal rites for Aichürök.
Let the great host of the Jediger,
All the Jediger people,
Come for the honor of taking a wife,
For the sake of giving the feast.
Send word to the people
For Khan Kyyaz’s glory:
To the elders who deem themselves great,
To all the tribal peoples,
To khans who are my peers and companions,
To those who will attend the celebration,
And to the children playing in the villages—
Let no old person remain behind;
Let all the teeming people come.
Let them see this spectacle of mine;
Let these people witness
The standing of the noble, unfortunate woman!
From distant Jelpinish at the earth’s end,
I shall summon every hero who can reach us;
From beyond Arman-Ayan, every giant who can cross,
I shall summon all who make the journey.
From lands where steeds grow weary and livestock falters,
I shall leave not a single one behind.
Of all whom ears have heard and eyes have seen,
I shall leave not a single person behind.
In the lowlands of Jeti-Özön,
For the feast of Lady Chürök,
I shall slaughter countless dark mares,
And innumerable camels;
I shall lay out wealth in equal measure.
I shall open all my livestock for the feast;
For the noble, unfortunate woman,
I shall send invitations through many cities.
In Köönö-Turpan and Bombai,
I shall feast all the peoples in sight
And show them wonders untold.
Facing the four directions,
I shall heap meat as high as jagged mountains,
And broth as broad as Ala-Köl;
I shall make the blue heavens roar
And set all who see it clamoring.
If I do not stage a spectacle before their eyes,
May I die unworthy of the name Khan Kyyaz!
If I do not make it a tale among the people,
May I sink without ever having been born!”
The many wrestlers who heard the decree
Slaughtered countless dark camels,
And countless black mares with white blazes;
They set wealth out in equal measure,
And slaughtered equally from all four kinds of livestock.
Kyyaz began the grand display,
Setting all the livestock and provisions
Out in the midst of the gathering.
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
With gold bound upon the horses,
With a clamor that split the sky,
Through the stratagem devised by Khan Kyyaz,
Word spread that Kyyaz had taken Aichürök.
The people’s uproar filled every conversation:
“Kyyaz slaughtered the bloodthirsty hero
And made spoil
Of his wife and child.”
His khanly fame rang among the people;
The blue heavens split with the noise,
And the people’s clamor filled the air.
It suited the Jediger well:
“This is Khan Kyyaz’s wedding,” they said.
The Jediger who filled Jeti-Özön
Streamed forth in excited crowds.
To see that feast,
Those without stallions rode camels,
And those without means went on foot;
The women hurried in noisy crowds,
And throngs of old women and old men
Stumbled along on their staffs;
The women walked in haste,
And the young men hurried,
All racing
To reach that feast.
Among the Jediger of Jeti-Özön,
No one wished to remain behind;
They all wanted to attend
The wedding of Kyyaz, who had taken a wife.
From Alty-Shaar and Margalang,
As far as Bukhara and Samarkand,
Above to Kokand and Andijan,
And before him to Margalang,
Kyyaz, warrior of the Jediger,
Sent greetings throughout the lands;
To peoples as far as his name was known,
He sent his greetings.
When they heard this news,
The people clamored in disbelief,
And the crowd buzzed at the strange affair.
All the judges grew stern,
And every khan bristled,
Speaking against warrior Kyyaz.
Many upright men,
Khans seated upon their thrones,
Those fit to govern peoples,
And mighty men who faced disaster,
Their hair standing on end,
Glared at warrior Kyyaz:
“Manas’s son, the great blood-shedding hero,
Possessed complete good fortune;
If you looked within that hero,
His heart was broader than the earth.
He never tormented a living soul,
Yet of all men ever born,
He never turned back in fear.
To say that from such a gray-maned hero
We have surrounded Talas
And seized his wife—
Look at the boastfulness
Of Kyyaz, son of Bagysh!
Look how he puffs himself up
And calls himself a giant!
Look how Kyyaz claims
To be master of the earth!
When he moves, his quarrel
Seems destined to reach all the peoples of the age,
As though when he stirs he could conquer
The whole world beyond the Kyrgyz.”
The people spoke in anger:
“Can one prosper by attacking
The people of Manas, father of the nation?
Can one slaughter the descendants
Of the true gray-maned hero?
He was renowned, a lion;
He was a noble, gray-maned champion,
A mountain pass that protected us
From the raging khakan.
He was the lion set over the people;
While the well-rooted descendants
Of the great-hearted hero stood watch,
What enemy could ever devour us?
He was a wrestler and a giant;
In every direction that blood-shedding hero
Was the champion who sheltered us.
Having lost the people’s mainstay,
Do we boast that we seized his livestock,
And congratulate ourselves
For taking his wife?
Look at swaggering Kyyaz—
Look how mad he has become!
Having killed the accomplished lion,
He has apparently become
Master of the lands and waters.
His white-blazed Jelerde was swift as wind,
And served as his mare.
Of every man who has gone beneath the earth,
This Kyyaz, here upon the earth,
He has apparently become their giant!
That vainglorious Kyyaz
Has apparently made himself
Master of every land he sees.
Yet the spirit of his forefather,
The lion Manas, has not vanished.
Kyyaz has set himself against Manas;
You shall see for yourself
That his undertaking will not prosper.
May that Kyyaz not belittle
Broad Keng-Köl and Talas,
Nor the majestic Manas who rests there.
This Jylgynduu, Keng-Köl,
And broad Talas
Are not lands where we dwell;
This leopard, the blood-shedding hero Manas,
Is not a hero we ourselves created.
His fame split the whole world;
We are but palm-sized beside Manas,
Whose warfare reached distant Beijing.
If they celebrate after taking his wife,
Will this great host of black-clad Jediger
Not meet with slaughter?
Were hilly Keng-Köl and broad Talas
A mountain pass one could cross without a word?
Was great-hearted, gray-maned Manas
A man whom anyone could attack?
This deed of Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
Is no ordinary act.
The Argyn and the Kyrgyz
Are not peoples for others to assail.
Warrior Kyyaz has gone mad;
This deed of his is no small thing.
In saying he will give a feast,
